name: Lonzo Cutright
equipment: Heavy coat: a rubberized mine coat, stiff with age
Walking stick, a hickory sounding rod with an iron tip, for tapping roof to hear whether it is drummy
A Wolf flame safety lamp of his own, for testing gas: the flame grows a blue cap in firedamp and dwindles and dies in blackdamp
The fire boss's book for No. 3, 1923 to date, every working place, every morning, his initials and the date
A box of white chalk, for marking the date and his initials at every face he has examined
A first-aid pouch: bandages, splints, a tourniquet, ammonia ampoules
A copy of the 1919 company map of 7 North, folded to a pad and soft as cloth, showing the face, the cross-cuts and the Number Two air shaft
features: Up Before Dawn (Farm-Raised origin: needs only 6 hours for a long rest; can't be surprised while awake in the last hour before sunrise; a fire boss's hours are three in the morning till noon, and he has kept them for twenty years)

There's an Explanation (Skeptic: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check, he names a rational cause aloud, squeeze, blackdamp, a pump knocking, a rat, and the failure becomes a success with no Dread; advantage on Investigation to find the mechanism behind anything that is a person's doing)

Careful Notes (Skeptic: once per short rest, after 10 minutes examining a working place, asks the GM 'What here has been moved?', 'Who was here most recently?' or 'What here does not fit?' and gets a true answer)

Calm Explanation (Skeptic, 2nd level: as an action, explains a frightening phenomenon to allies who can hear him; until the end of the scene they have advantage on fear checks against that one horror; once per long rest)

Discipline: Scientist (Skeptic, 3rd level: with his safety lamp, an anemometer and a long rest he can rig instruments, and the GM tells him honestly what they record: the air, gas, temperature, whether a door was opened; advantage on Mechanics checks with instruments)
Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: pumps, fans, motors, lamps; a few minutes with a machine tells him what is wrong with it, including whether someone made it go wrong)

personality.traits: I say 'I couldn't say' when I can say. I tap every roof I walk under. I'm the most careful man in the mine and I am proud of it, and every morning I write it down.
personality.ideals: The mine will kill you if you let it. A fire boss is the man who goes in first, alone, with a lamp, and comes back out and says it's safe, and if he's wrong men die. I believed for twenty years that meant I was a good man.
personality.bonds: The men who go in after me every morning. My wife Ruth and the farm in Lincoln County I'm saving to buy back. The fourteen, whom I helped wall in.
personality.flaws: I was on the seal crew in 1919. I heard them knocking. I laid block anyway, because Bledsoe said the fire would take the mine and every man's job, and then said the knocking was squeeze, and I let him tell me. I wrote a letter to a Pittsburgh paper and didn't sign it. I am a coward who goes into the dark alone every morning, and I know exactly how that sounds.

appearance: A spare, slightly bent man of forty-nine with a lined grey face, a short grey beard, pale eyes red-rimmed from the lamp, and the miner's blue scars on his knuckles. A stiff mine coat, a hard-toed boot on one foot and a split one on the other, a safety lamp on his belt and a sounding rod in his hand.
backstory: Lonzo Cutright grew up on a Lincoln County farm that the bank took in 1904, and went into the mines to get it back, and never did. He is a certified fire boss, and for the last eight years his job has been to walk every working place in Ottway No. 3 between three and six every morning, alone, with a flame safety lamp, testing for gas and bad roof, and to chalk his initials and the date at each face before a single man goes in. He is very good at it and has not lost a man. In October 1919 he was a section foreman, and Elwood Bledsoe put him in charge of the seven-man crew that built the two seals across 7 North. They heard the knocking on the second day: four and two, the old signal for men alive. Bledsoe came down and listened, and said it was squeeze, the mountain settling on a fire, and that if the seals weren't finished the fire would take the whole mine, and they finished them. On the 17th the knocking was still coming, and Lonzo went to Bledsoe's office, and Bledsoe showed him a telegram from Philadelphia and said they had capped the air shaft that morning. Every man on the crew got fifty dollars in scrip. On the night of 28 March 1927, testing at the 7 North seal, he heard the knocking again, faint and slow: four, then two. He told Bledsoe, who told him it was squeeze. On 30 March, in Gale, he wrote the letter. At 3:10 on the morning of Monday 11 April, he will hear it again, louder, and close.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Lonzo is the company man with a conscience and the fastest way to the truth, if the party can make it safe for him to tell it. He carries CLUE A1 (the knocking at the seal, which he reports to Bledsoe and, if he trusts them, to the party), C3 (his fire-boss book: from 2 March, lamps going blue in the 7 North entries with no gas on the instrument, and the mules refusing the main heading) and E5 (his own confession), and he has the 1919 map. He is the best guide underground the party can have, and he knows both seals, the old Shumate hole-through and the air shaft's position to the foot. He will not confess while he thinks it will cost the other seal-crew men their jobs; he will confess at once if Dewey Spradlin is still alive and there is a way to get him out.
dmNotes.voice: Slow, dry, few words; a farm voice. Answers questions with measurements. When frightened, gets more precise, not less: 'That's eleven feet of roof and it's working.'
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: get Dewey out alive, which would undo something. Secondary: keep the seal-crew men from being blamed for what Bledsoe and Philadelphia decided. Tertiary: keep his certificate and his job.
dmNotes.secrets: He wrote the anonymous letter to the Allegheny Labor Herald, in pencil on store paper, and posted it in Gale on 30 March; Frankie Lowry's Detective feature or any comparison of handwriting with his fire-boss book proves it. He also knows that Superintendent Bledsoe has kept four of the fourteen brass checks in the bottom drawer of his desk since 1 March, because Lonzo saw him take them out of the bucket.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: polite, unhelpful, watchful, until one of them goes underground with him and keeps their head. Toward Bledsoe: loyalty worn to a thread. Toward Lettie Burchett: shame; he carried Wash's coffin. Toward Captain Kincaid: dislike, which he hides. Toward Morris Pettaway: he cannot look him in the face.
